name: Dating-profile photo optimization
lead: Dating-profile photo optimization is the practice of selecting, editing and ordering photographs for dating apps using feedback or data, rather than personal preference alone. In looksmaxxing communities it is most often associated with Photofeeler, a site where anonymous voters rate photos on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness.[1][2]

Proponents say outside ratings reveal how strangers perceive a photo, since friends and family may give overly positive opinions.[2] Forum members also report cases where rated-highest photos did poorly on dating apps, and criticism that raters favour smiling expressions.[3][4]
No independent studies were found testing whether Photofeeler-optimised photos increase dating-app matches.

paras: The practice involves choosing which photos to use on a dating profile, and in what order, by testing them with strangers. Photofeeler's dating test asks voters to rate a photo on smartness, trustworthiness and attractiveness.[1] Grokipedia says the site's founders wanted objective feedback because friends and family tend to be overly positive.[2]

Photofeeler reports scores adjusted for voter tendencies and standardised within gender and age groups, and offers comments from voters.[2] The company has published analyses of its own data, including a 2014 study of business photos and a 2019 neural network paper trained on 1.2 million dating photos.[1]

Members of looksmax.org share Photofeeler scores and debate their usefulness. Reported complaints include a mismatch between rater scores and Tinder results and a perceived bias toward smiling photos.[3] Others compare results across voter-age and gender settings.[4][5]

lore.intro: Photofeeler is the main reference point; forum members dispute how well its scores predict dating-app performance.[3][5]

claims.claim: Rated-best photos do not necessarily perform best on dating apps
claims.believers: A poster said his highest-rated photo did poorly on Tinder while his lowest-rated did well.[3]
claims.experts: No published study compares Photofeeler scores with dating-app outcomes.

claims.believers: Members say serious photos are marked down with requests to smile.[3]
claims.experts: Photofeeler's own 2014 business-photo analysis found that a smile showing teeth gave the largest boost to likability.[1]

card.summary: Picking and ordering dating photos with data from strangers' votes; popular idea, little independent testing.
card.note: Forum reports of rated-best photos underperforming on apps are anecdotal.

quick.overview:
This is the practice of testing dating-app photos, usually with Photofeeler ratings, before choosing which to use. Supporters say it reveals how strangers see a photo.

Evidence is limited: the research comes from the company itself, and forum members report mixed real-world results.
quick.mechanism: People upload candidate photos to a rating site, compare scores on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness, and pick or order photos accordingly.[1]
quick.risks: Low physical risk. Reported drawbacks are bias toward certain expressions, discouraging scores, and sharing photos with strangers.[3]
